name: Anu-Hkongso
confidence_why: 5 independent first-hand sources agree (2 agree, 2 refine), none contradicts

new_statements.quote: Khongso exhibits a rhythmic pattern consisting of combinations of minor and major syllables in an iambic pattern (unstressed-stressed) which is typical of languages of mainland Southeast Asia, including Mon-Khmer languages, Thai, and Burmese [...]. Initial elements of polysyllabic constructions tend to be shorter due to this rhythmic pattern. [p. 531-532] [...] Other polysyllabic words, such as trisyllabic words, are similar in that they contain reduced syllables followed by a major ultimate syllable. [p. 532] [...] However, /ə/ primarily occurs in unstressed syllables. As Khongso has a sesquisyllabic word structure, these are typically the first syllable in disyllabic words. [p. 528]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's final placement (final stress = stress on the last syllable in 2- and 3-syllable words) and adds the mechanism: sesquisyllabic iambic word shape with reduced, mid-toned minor syllables before a major final syllable carrying the full five-tone contrast; adds the compound exception and duration measurements.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mostly monosyllabic; disyllabic words are sesquisyllabic (a reduced 'minor' syllable, Cə or a syllabic nasal with only a level mid tone, followed by a full 'major' syllable) and longer words likewise have reduced syllables followed by a major ultimate syllable. Word rhythm is iambic (unstressed-stressed), so stress falls on the final (major) syllable; the language also has five contrastive lexical tones, which are carried by major syllables while non-final syllables of polysyllabic words neutralize to a level mid tone (p. 531). Note: the article has no subsection titled 'Stress'; the placement statement is made through the terms 'iambic (unstressed-stressed)', 'unstressed syllables' and 'major ultimate syllable'. The text layer renders the IPA-font schwa in '/ə/ primarily occurs in unstressed syllables' as '/´/'; the glyph is schwa (cf. 'diagrammed as CIə', p. 532).
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds whose parts are recoverable can have two full syllables (i˦-mi˦ '1PL-people (person)', p. 531), i.e. no reduced first syllable there; minor syllables are ~0.10 s vs significantly longer major syllables (p. 532); mid-falling tone often creaky; tones reported resistant to sandhi but 'not entirely immutable' (p. 531).
new_statements.identity_note: Wright 2020 describes Khongso (Hkongso), spoken by 2-3 thousand people in 17 villages along the Michaung River, Paletwa Township, Southern Chin State, Myanmar; data from speakers in or travelling to Yangon plus village recordings by Khongso assistants. The article states Khongso is mutually intelligible with Anu (about 700 speakers, west of the Khongso area) and that both share ISO anl and glottocode anuu1241; the description is of the Khongso variety, not Anu proper. Not a tone-vs-stress conflict: the language is tonal (five lexical tones) and has final word stress with a reduced initial minor syllable.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final stress (final stress)' rests on Wright 2009, the sole grammar sketch of Anu-Hkongso and the only descriptive work Glottolog lists; the deciding sentence is verbatim at sec. 2.3.2 p. 30. The one later source, Wright's 2020/2022 JIPA Illustration (downloaded now, open from Cambridge Core), independently restates iambic minor+major word rhythm with reduced non-final syllables and a full 'major ultimate syllable', backed by duration measurements, so nothing suggests the classification is wrong. Weaknesses are bookkeeping, not substance: the record held no file and its grade field is blank; both PDFs are now under Action: register the held thesis, add the JIPA paper as corroborating citation, and set the strength of the evidence accordingly.
